name: Erythrulose

lead: Erythrulose is a small sugar used in sunless tanning products, usually together with DHA. It is described as giving a gradual, bronze-toned colour.
No clinical studies of its tanning effect were found.

paras: It is described as reacting with amino acids in the outer skin layer (a Maillard-type reaction) to form brown pigments, more slowly than DHA.
The sources reviewed contain no safety or regulatory data specific to erythrulose.

lead: Erythrulose is a four-carbon ketose sugar (a tetrose) found naturally in fruits such as raspberries and used in cosmetics as a sunless tanning ingredient.[1][2] It is usually produced by microbial fermentation.[1]

As a tanning agent it is described as reacting with amino acids in the outer skin layer in a Maillard-type reaction to give a gradual brown colour, and it is commonly combined with dihydroxyacetone (DHA) in self-tanners to affect colour development and evenness.[1] No clinical trials of its tanning performance were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: Erythrulose has the formula C4H8O4 and a molar mass of about 120 g/mol; it is the only ketotetrose and exists as D and L forms. It can be made by enzyme-mediated condensation of glycolaldehyde.[1][2]

According to Grokipedia, a reference text that may contain errors, erythrulose reacts with amino groups in keratin to form brown pigments (melanoidins), reacts more slowly than DHA, and is blended with DHA in formulas to improve evenness and wear.[1] It is supplied as an aqueous syrup of roughly 80% active material.[1] Independent clinical data and regulatory documents were not available among the sources reviewed.
